questions.question: What is the main difference between air quality and the Air Quality Index (AQI)?

options.text: Air quality is a measure of noise pollution, while the Air Quality Index (AQI) is an index for public awareness.
Air quality represents absolute pollution levels, while the Air Quality Index (AQI) is an index for public awareness.
Air quality is only measured in cities, while the Air Quality Index (AQI) is an index for public awareness.
Air quality is used for scientific research, while the Air Quality Index (AQI) is an index for public awareness.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Air quality represents absolute pollution levels, while the Air Quality Index (AQI) is an index for public awareness.**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Air quality** refers to the physical and chemical condition of the ambient air, specifically the concentration of various pollutants present in it. It is measured in **absolute scientific units** such as micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) or parts per million (ppm).

• The **Air Quality Index (AQI)** is a communication tool used by government agencies to simplify complex scientific data into a single number, color, and description. Its primary goal is to promote **public awareness** regarding how local air quality affects health.

• The main difference lies in their application: **Air quality** provides the raw data on **absolute pollution levels**, whereas the **AQI** translates that data into a scale that helps the general public understand health risks and take necessary precautions.

• While air quality data is essential for **scientific research** and environmental monitoring, the AQI is specifically designed to be a **public-facing index**.

**Additional Information__**

• In India, the **National Air Quality Index (NAQI)** was launched in **October 2014** under the **Swachh Bharat Abhiyan** to provide a 'One Number-One Color-One Description' system.

• The **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)** monitors air quality across the country. The Indian AQI considers **eight major pollutants**: Particulate Matter (**PM10** and **PM2.5**), Nitrogen Dioxide (**NO2**), Sulfur Dioxide (**SO2**), Carbon Monoxide (**CO**), Ozone (**O3**), Ammonia (**NH3**), and Lead (**Pb**).

• The AQI scale in India ranges from **0 to 500**, categorized into six levels: **Good** (0–50), **Satisfactory** (51–100), **Moderately Polluted** (101–200), **Poor** (201–300), **Very Poor** (301–400), and **Severe** (401–500).

• High levels of **PM2.5** are particularly dangerous as these fine particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, causing respiratory and cardiovascular diseases.

questions.question: What is the elasticity of supply called when a proportionate change in supply is more than a proportionate change in price?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Relatively elastic supply**__.

• **Relatively elastic supply** occurs when the **percentage change in quantity supplied** is **greater than** the **percentage change in price**. In this scenario, the **Price Elasticity of Supply (Es)** is **greater than 1** (Es > 1).

• This type of elasticity indicates that producers are highly responsive to **price fluctuations**. Even a small **increase in price** leads to a significantly larger **increase in the quantity** that firms are willing to bring to the **market**.

• The **supply curve** for a relatively elastic supply is typically **flatter**. When the curve is extended, it intersects the **Price axis (Y-axis)**, which mathematically represents an **elasticity coefficient** higher than unity.

• For example, if the **price** of a product increases by **10%** and the **quantity supplied** rises by **25%**, the **elasticity** is calculated as 25/10 = **2.5**. Since 2.5 is **greater than 1**, the supply is considered **relatively elastic**.

questions.question: The ISRO satellite series, used mainly for meteorological and weather forecasting purposes, is:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**INSAT**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **INSAT (Indian National Satellite System)** is a series of multipurpose geostationary satellites launched by **ISRO** to satisfy the telecommunications, broadcasting, **meteorology**, and search and rescue needs of **India**. It is the primary satellite series used for **weather forecasting** and monitoring atmospheric conditions. ***Hence, option 1 is correct.***

• The **INSAT** system was established in **1983** with the commissioning of **INSAT-1B**. It is a joint venture of the **Department of Space (DOS)**, **Department of Telecommunications**, **India Meteorological Department (IMD)**, **All India Radio (AIR)**, and **Doordarshan**.

• Specific satellites like **INSAT-3D** and **INSAT-3DR** are currently operational and carry advanced **multi-spectral imagers** and **sounders**. These instruments provide vertical profiles of temperature and humidity, which are crucial for accurate **weather forecasting** and **cyclone tracking**.

• **RISAT (Radar Imaging Satellite)** is a series of **Indian remote sensing satellites** that use **Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR)** to provide all-weather surveillance. While it can see through clouds, its primary use is for **agriculture**, **forestry**, and **disaster management** imaging rather than general meteorological forecasting. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• **Cartosat** is a series of **Earth observation satellites** used specifically for **cartography** (mapping). They provide high-resolution images used for **urban planning**, **coastal land use**, and **Land Information Systems (LIS)**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• **IRNSS (Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System)**, commercially known as **NavIC**, is an independent regional navigation satellite system designed to provide accurate position information services to users in **India**. It functions similarly to the **Global Positioning System (GPS)**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**

__

• **ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation)**: Founded by **Dr. Vikram Sarabhai** on **15 August 1969**, it is headquartered in **Bengaluru**. It is the primary agency in **India** for space research and planetary exploration.

• **Kalpana-1**: This was the first exclusive **meteorological satellite** launched by **ISRO** on **September 12, 2002**. Originally named **METSAT-1**, it was renamed in honor of the **Indian-American** astronaut **Kalpana Chawla**, who perished in the **Columbia Space Shuttle** disaster.

• **NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation)**: This system consists of a constellation of **7 satellites**. It provides two types of services: **Standard Positioning Service (SPS)** for civilian users and **Restricted Service (RS)** for authorized users like the **Indian Armed Forces**.

• **Remote Sensing**: **India** has one of the largest constellations of remote sensing satellites in operation today, including the **Resourcesat**, **Oceansat**, and **Scatsat** series, which help in monitoring **natural resources** and **oceanic winds**.

**Important Points__**

• The **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** utilizes data from the **INSAT** series at its **Meteorological Data Utilization Centre (MDUC)** located in **New Delhi**. This data is vital for issuing **early warnings** for **tsunamis**, **floods**, and **heavy rainfall**.

• **INSAT-3DR**, launched in **2016**, carries a **Data Relay Transponder (DRT)**. This component is used to receive **meteorological**, **hydrological**, and **oceanographic** data from remote and uninhabited locations through **Automatic Data Collection Platforms (ADCPs)**.

• The **GSAT** series is another important satellite family from **ISRO**, which focuses primarily on **digital audio**, **data**, and **video broadcasting**, complementing the communication capabilities of the **INSAT** series.
</ul

questions.question: Which government scheme aims to provide affordable and quality healthcare through a network of primary health centers and other facilities?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**National Rural Health Mission (NHM)**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **National Health Mission (NHM)** is the primary government initiative aimed at providing affordable, accessible, and quality healthcare through a vast network of facilities. It was launched by the **Ministry of Health and Family Welfare** to address the healthcare needs of both rural and urban populations. ***Hence, option 3 is the correct answer.***

• The mission is divided into two sub-missions: the **National Rural Health Mission (NRHM)**, launched on **12th April 2005**, and the **National Urban Health Mission (NUHM)**, launched in **2013**.

• The core strategy of **NHM** involves strengthening the public health delivery system by improving the infrastructure of **Sub-Centres (SCs)**, **Primary Health Centres (PHCs)**, and **Community Health Centres (CHCs)**. It ensures that these facilities meet the **Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS)**.

• A key feature of the **NRHM** is the introduction of the **Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA)**, a trained female community health volunteer who acts as the first point of contact for any health-related demands of the rural population, particularly women and children.

• The mission focuses on achieving major health indicators such as reducing the **Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR)** to **1 per 1000 live births**, the **Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)** to **25 per 1000 live births**, and the **Total Fertility Rate (TFR)** to **2.1**.

**Additional Information__**

• **Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM)**: Launched in **October 2021**, this scheme is one of the largest pan-India schemes for strengthening healthcare infrastructure. Its primary goal is to fill critical gaps in public health infrastructure, surveillance, and health research. It aims to establish **Integrated Public Health Labs** in all **730 districts** and set up **Critical Care Hospital Blocks** in over **600 districts**.

• **Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY)**: This scheme was announced in **2003** with the objective of correcting regional imbalances in the availability of affordable and reliable **tertiary healthcare services**. It involves the setting up of **AIIMS-like institutions** (such as **AIIMS Rishikesh**, **AIIMS Bhopal**, etc.) and the upgradation of existing **Government Medical Colleges (GMCs)** by adding super-specialty blocks.

• **Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK)**: Launched on **1st June 2011**, this initiative aims to eliminate out-of-pocket expenses for **pregnant women** and **sick newborns**. It entitles all pregnant women delivering in public health institutions to **free delivery**, including **Caesarean sections**, free drugs, diagnostics, diet, and free transport from home to the facility.

• **Ayushman Bharat - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY)**: Launched in **September 2018**, it is the world’s largest health insurance scheme fully financed by the government. It provides a cover of **Rs. 5 lakhs** per family per year for **secondary and tertiary care** hospitalization to over **12 crore** poor and vulnerable families (approximately **55 crore beneficiaries**).

• **National Health Policy (NHP) 2017**: This policy serves as the guiding framework for these schemes, aiming to increase government health expenditure to **2.5% of GDP** by **2025** and ensuring **Universal Health Coverage (UHC)** for all citizens.

questions.question: A transformer works on the principle of:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• A **transformer** is a static electrical device that transfers electrical energy from one alternating-current circuit to another through the process of **mutual induction**.

• The fundamental principle behind its operation is **Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction**, which states that a time-varying magnetic flux through a loop induces an **electromotive force (EMF)** in that loop.

• In a transformer, an **alternating current** flowing through the **primary coil** creates a varying magnetic field in the core. This changing magnetic flux links with the **secondary coil**, inducing a voltage across its terminals.

• **Ohm's Law** (V = IR) describes the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance in a conductor but does not explain the transfer of energy between isolated circuits.

• **Lenz's Law** determines the **direction** of the induced EMF and current such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it; it is a consequence of the law of conservation of energy.

• **Conservation of Charge** states that the total electric charge in an isolated system remains constant, which is a general physical principle but not the specific operational mechanism of a transformer.

**Additional Information__**

• Transformers are used to **Step-up** (increase) or **Step-down** (decrease) voltage levels in power systems while maintaining the same **frequency**.

• A transformer cannot work on **Direct Current (DC)** because DC produces a constant magnetic field, which results in zero change in flux and thus no induced EMF in the secondary winding.

• The relationship between the primary and secondary voltages and the number of turns is given by the transformer ratio: **Vₚ / Vₛ = Nₚ / Nₛ**.

• An **Ideal Transformer** is assumed to have no losses (no copper loss, iron loss, or flux leakage), meaning the input power equals the output power.

• The core of a transformer is usually made of **laminated silicon steel** to reduce energy losses caused by **eddy currents** and **hysteresis**.
</ul

questions.question: Who was the Finance Minister of India when the First Five-Year Plan was introduced?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**C.D. Deshmukh**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **C.D. Deshmukh** (Chintaman Dwarakanath Deshmukh) was the **Finance Minister of India** from **1950 to 1956**, covering the entire duration when the **First Five-Year Plan** was introduced and implemented.

• The **First Five-Year Plan** was launched for the period **1951 to 1956**. While Prime Minister **Jawaharlal Nehru** presented the plan to the **Parliament of India** in **December 1951**, the financial allocations and budgetary support were overseen by **C.D. Deshmukh**.

• **John Mathai** (Option 4) served as the **Finance Minister** from **1948 to 1950**. He resigned shortly after the **Planning Commission** was set up in **1950** due to disagreements over its role and powers, making him the predecessor to **C.D. Deshmukh**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

• **T.T. Krishnamachari** (Option 3) served as the **Finance Minister** twice, first from **1956 to 1958** and later from **1963 to 1965**. He succeeded **C.D. Deshmukh** after the latter resigned over the issue of the reorganization of states. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• **Morarji Desai** (Option 1) served as the **Finance Minister** much later, starting in **1958**, and holds the record for presenting the maximum number of **Union Budgets (10)**. He also served as the **4th Prime Minister of India**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• **C.D. Deshmukh** was a distinguished **Indian Civil Service (ICS)** officer and was the first Indian to be appointed as the **Governor of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** in **1943**. ***Hence, the correct answer is C.D. Deshmukh.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **First Five-Year Plan (1951–1956):** This plan was based on the **Harrod-Domar model**, which emphasized the role of savings and investment in economic growth. It primarily focused on the **agricultural sector**, including **irrigation** and **power projects**, to overcome the food crisis following **Independence** and **Partition**.

• **Economic Achievements:** The plan was a great success, achieving a **growth rate of 3.6%**, which was significantly higher than the initial **target of 2.1%**. During this period, major dams like the **Bhakra Nangal**, **Hirakud**, and **Mettur Dam** were initiated.

• **Planning Commission:** It was established on **15 March 1950** as a non-constitutional and advisory body. The **Prime Minister** acted as the **Ex-officio Chairman**. It has since been replaced by **NITI Aayog** (National Institution for Transforming India) on **1 January 2015**.

• **Bretton Woods Conference:** **C.D. Deshmukh** represented India at the **Bretton Woods Conference** in **1944**, which led to the creation of the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** and the **World Bank**.

• **Social Sector:** At the end of the plan period in **1956**, five **Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs)** were started as major technical institutions. The **University Grants Commission (UGC)** was also set up to take care of funding and take measures to strengthen higher education in the country.

**Important Points__**

• **Key Figures:** **K.N. Raj**, a young economist, is often regarded as one of the main architects of the **First Five-Year Plan**.

• **National Income:** During the first plan, the **National Income** increased by **18%** and the **Per Capita Income** rose by **11%**.

• **Community Development Programme:** Launched in **1952**, it was one of the most significant steps toward **rural development** during the first plan period.

• **C.D. Deshmukh's Legacy:** Apart from his role in finance, he served as the **Vice-Chancellor of Delhi University** and the **Chairman of the UGC**. He was awarded the **Bharat Ratna** (posthumously) and the **Ramon Magsaysay Award** for Government Service in **1959**.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about nucleases and DNA polymerase I is INCORRECT?

options.text: Exonucleases remove the nucleotides from the ends
DNA Pol I does not have a 5'-to-3' exonuclease activity
First polymerase isolated in E. coli was DNA Pol I

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**DNA Pol I does not have a 5'-to-3' exonuclease activity**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **DNA Polymerase I (Pol I)** is a multifunctional enzyme that possesses three distinct activities: 5'-to-3' polymerase activity, 3'-to-5' exonuclease activity (for **proofreading**), and **5'-to-3' exonuclease activity**.

• The **5'-to-3' exonuclease activity** is a unique feature of DNA Pol I among the major E. coli polymerases, allowing it to remove **RNA primers** and replace them with DNA during replication and repair. Therefore, the statement that it lacks this activity is **incorrect**.

• **Exonucleases** are enzymes that catalyze the removal of nucleotides one by one from the **termini (ends)** of a DNA or RNA molecule.

• **Endonucleases** are enzymes that make cuts at specific or non-specific positions **internally** within the DNA strand, rather than at the ends.

• **DNA Polymerase I** was the **first DNA polymerase** to be isolated and characterized from **Escherichia coli** by **Arthur Kornberg** in 1956, for which he received the Nobel Prize.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Klenow fragment** is a large protein fragment produced when DNA Pol I is enzymatically cleaved by proteases like subtilisin; it retains the 5'-to-3' polymerase and 3'-to-5' exonuclease activities but **loses the 5'-to-3' exonuclease activity**.

• While DNA Pol I is essential for **DNA repair** and processing **Okazaki fragments**, **DNA Polymerase III** is the primary enzyme responsible for the bulk of **DNA replication** in E. coli.

• The 3'-to-5' exonuclease activity is critical for **high-fidelity** replication as it allows the enzyme to remove mismatched bases immediately after they are incorporated.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following has been decriminalized as per the BNS, 2023?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Attempt to suicide**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023**, which replaced the **Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860**, has effectively **decriminalized** the general act of **attempting suicide**.

• Under the old **IPC**, **Section 309** categorized the attempt to commit suicide as a criminal offense punishable with imprisonment or a fine.

• The **BNS, 2023** has omitted the equivalent of Section 309, acknowledging that individuals attempting suicide often require **medical and psychological support** rather than criminal prosecution.

• However, the BNS introduces **Section 226**, which specifically penalizes an attempt to commit suicide only if it is done with the intent to **compel or restrain a public servant** from discharging their official duty.

• Other options like **Voyeurism** (Section 77), **Domestic Violence** (Section 85 and 86), and **Cyberstalking** (Section 78) remain serious criminal offenses under the new legal framework.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017**, through **Section 115**, had already significantly reduced the impact of Section 309 IPC by creating a presumption of **severe stress** for anyone attempting suicide.

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita** received the President's assent on **December 25, 2023**, and came into force on **July 1, 2024**.

• The shift in law reflects a **humanitarian approach** toward mental health issues in India's criminal justice system.

• The BNS also introduced **Community Service** as a form of punishment for the first time for petty offenses.
</ul

questions.question: What is a common theme in Sattriya dance performances?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Devotion to Krishna**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Sattriya** is a major **Indian classical dance** form that originated in the **Sattras** (monasteries) of **Assam**. It was introduced by the great **Vaishnava saint** and reformer **Mahapurush Sankaradeva** in the **15th century AD**.

• The theme of **Warfare** is typically associated with martial dance forms such as **Chhau** or **Kalaripayattu**, rather than the spiritual essence of **Sattriya**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• **Agricultural rituals** form the basis of various folk dances like **Bihu**, which is also from **Assam**, but **Sattriya** is strictly a ritualistic and devotional classical dance. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• The most common and central theme of **Sattriya** performances is **Devotion to Krishna**. The dance usually narrates stories of **Lord Krishna** and his divine acts (**Leelas**) as described in the **Bhagavata Purana**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***

• **Courtly love** is a frequent theme in other classical dances like **Kathak** or **Odissi**, which flourished in royal courts, whereas **Sattriya** remained confined to the monastic **Sattras** for centuries. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

• The dance was traditionally performed by male monks, known as **Bhokots**, as part of their daily spiritual practice and to celebrate religious festivals.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Sattriya** was officially recognized as one of the **eight classical dance forms** of India by the **Sangeet Natak Akademi** on **15 November 2000**.

• The musical foundation of the dance is based on **Borgeets**, which are devotional songs composed by **Sankaradeva** and his disciple **Madhavadeva** in a unique language called **Brajavali**.

• Traditional musical instruments used in **Sattriya** include the **Khol** (a two-faced drum), **Cymbals** (Manjira or Tala), and the **Flute**. The rhythmic patterns, known as **Taals**, are highly sophisticated.

• The costumes are made from **Assam Silk**, specifically **Pat Silk**, and feature traditional motifs like the **Kingkhap**. Male dancers wear a **Dhoti** and **Paguri** (turban), while female dancers wear **Ghuri** and **Chadar**.

• The dance includes various sub-genres such as **Apsara Nritya**, **Behar Nritya**, **Chali Nritya**, and **Jhumura**, each with its own specific movements and spiritual significance.

**Important Points__**

• **Ankiya Nat**: These are traditional one-act plays that serve as the narrative core for **Sattriya** dance. They were designed by **Sankaradeva** to spread the **Bhakti movement** among the masses.

• **Sattras**: These are **Vaishnavite monasteries** that have preserved the **Sattriya** tradition for over **500 years**. The river island of **Majuli** is the most prominent hub for these institutions.

• **Ekasarana Dharma**: This is the monotheistic **Vaishnava** philosophy propagated by **Sankaradeva**, which emphasizes total surrender and **Devotion to Krishna** (or **Vishnu**) as the sole deity.

• **Modern Evolution**: While it was once a strictly monastic tradition performed only by men, **Sattriya** has evolved in the **20th century** to include female performers and is now showcased on global stages.
</ul

questions.question:
Which of the given statements is /are CORRECT?

1. Soil erosion and deforestation over a long period may convert arable land into a wasteland.
2. India has the largest land under plain areas as compared to Mountains and plateaus.
3. The net sown area in India is similar in all the states, excluding the North-Eastern states.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1 and 2 only**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1**: **Soil erosion** and **deforestation** are primary drivers of **land degradation**. When protective vegetation is removed and topsoil is washed away by **wind** or **water** over a long period, the land loses its fertility and moisture-retaining capacity. This process eventually converts **arable land** into **wasteland**, making it unfit for **agriculture**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Statement 2**: India possesses diverse **relief features**. Approximately **43%** of the land area is **plain**, which provides facilities for **agriculture** and **industry**. **Mountains** account for **30%** of the total surface area, ensuring the perennial flow of some rivers and providing facilities for **tourism** and **ecology**. About **27%** of the area is the **plateau** region, which possesses rich reserves of **minerals**, **fossil fuels**, and **forests**. Since **43%** is the largest proportion, plains are the dominant relief feature. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• **Statement 3**: The pattern of **net sown area** varies greatly from one state to another. It is over **80%** of the total area in **Punjab** and **Haryana**, but it is less than **10%** in **Arunachal Pradesh**, **Mizoram**, **Manipur**, and the **Andaman Nicobar Islands**. This variation is not limited only to **North-Eastern states** but is seen across various regions due to **topography**, **climate**, and **soil types**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is 1 and 2 only.***

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Land Use Pattern in India:**
 
 
• The use of land is determined both by **physical factors** such as **topography**, **climate**, **soil types** as well as **human factors** such as **population density**, **technological capability**, and **culture** and **traditions**.
 
• The total **geographical area** of **India** is **3.28 million square km**. However, **land use data** is available only for **93%** of the total area because reporting for most of the **North-East states** (except **Assam**) and some parts of **Jammu and Kashmir** has not been fully conducted.
 
• The **forest area** in the country is far lower than the desired **33%** of geographical area, as outlined in the **National Forest Policy (1952)**.
 
 
 
• **Land Degradation and Conservation:**
 
 
• At present, there are about **130 million hectares** of **degraded land** in **India**. Approximately **28%** of it belongs to the category of **forest degraded area**, **56%** is **water eroded area**, and the rest is affected by **saline** and **alkaline deposits**.
 
• Human activities such as **deforestation**, **overgrazing**, **mining**, and **quarrying** have contributed significantly to **land degradation**.
 
• In states like **Jharkhand**, **Chhattisgarh**, **Madhya Pradesh**, and **Odisha**, **deforestation** due to **mining** has caused severe land degradation.
 
• In states like **Gujarat**, **Rajasthan**, **Madhya Pradesh**, and **Maharashtra**, **overgrazing** is one of the main reasons for land degradation.
 
• In the states of **Punjab**, **Haryana**, and western **Uttar Pradesh**, **over-irrigation** is responsible for land degradation due to **waterlogging** leading to increase in **salinity** and **alkalinity** in the soil.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• **Fallow Lands:** These are lands left without cultivation for one or less than one agricultural year to allow the soil to regain its fertility.
 
• **Culturable Wasteland:** Land left uncultivated for more than **5 agricultural years**.
 
• **Net Sown Area:** The physical extent of land on which crops are sown and harvested is known as **net sown area**.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: Read the below statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Mark the correct options:**Assertion (A):** Victorian Gothic buildings near Mumbai's Oval Maidan include Indian features like sloping tiled roofs and verandas.**Reason (R):** They were built using local basalt and Porbandar limestone, allowing integration of climate-suited features with Gothic style.

options.text: Both A and R are correct, and R explains A
Both A and R are correct, but R does not explain A
A is correct, R is incorrect
A is incorrect, R is correct

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both A and R are correct, and R explains A**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Assertion (A)** states that **Victorian Gothic** buildings near **Mumbai's Oval Maidan** include Indian features like **sloping tiled roofs** and **verandas**. This is correct because the **Gothic Revival** style, imported from **Europe** in the **19th century**, had to be adapted to the **tropical climate** of **India**. The **sloping roofs** were essential to drain the heavy **monsoon** rainwater, while **verandas** and **balconies** provided necessary shade and cross-ventilation. *Hence, statement A is correct.*

• **Reason (R)** explains that these buildings were constructed using local materials like **basalt** (specifically **Kurla basalt**) and **Porbandar limestone**. The availability of these local stones allowed architects to integrate **climate-suited features** into the **Gothic** framework. The **basalt** provided a sturdy, dark foundation, while the **limestone** allowed for intricate carvings and the creation of open galleries and **verandas** that are characteristic of Indian domestic architecture. *Hence, statement R is correct.*

• The **Reason (R)** directly explains **Assertion (A)** because the choice of **local materials** and the technical flexibility they offered enabled the **British architects** and **Indian craftsmen** to modify the rigid **European Gothic** designs. This synthesis created a unique architectural language known as **Bombay Gothic** or **Indo-Gothic**, where the structural logic of the **Gothic** style was successfully merged with **Indian** environmental needs. *Therefore, R is the correct explanation of A.*

• The buildings facing the **Oval Maidan**, such as the **Bombay High Court** and the **University of Mumbai**, serve as primary examples of this adaptation. They represent a period of **urban expansion** in the **1860s** and **1870s** following the demolition of the **Fort walls**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **UNESCO World Heritage Status**: The **Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai** were officially inscribed as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in **July 2018**. This ensemble includes **19th-century Victorian Gothic** public buildings and **20th-century Art Deco** residential buildings around the **Oval Maidan**.

• **Architectural Features**: The **Victorian Gothic** style in **Mumbai** is characterized by **pointed arches**, **ribbed vaults**, and **flying buttresses**. However, the **Indian** influence added **carvings** of local flora and fauna, **wooden shutters**, and **deep eaves** to protect against the **sun** and **rain**.

• **Key Architects**: Prominent architects like **Sir George Gilbert Scott** (who designed the **University Library** and **Rajabai Clock Tower**) and **Colonel James Fuller** (who designed the **High Court**) were instrumental in shaping this skyline. The **Rajabai Tower**, standing at **280 feet**, was modeled after **Big Ben** in **London** but incorporated **oriental** motifs.

• **Materials Used**: The use of **Kurla basalt** (a dark grey stone) and **Malad stone** (a buff-colored stone) created a distinctive **polychromatic** effect. **Porbandar limestone** from **Gujarat** was frequently used for decorative elements due to its relative softness and ease of carving.

• **Historical Context**: This architectural movement flourished under the governorship of **Sir Bartle Frere** (**1862–1867**), who envisioned **Bombay** as a **Urbs Prima in Indis** (The First City in India). The wealth generated from the **Cotton Trade** during the **American Civil War** provided the **funding** for these grand projects.

**Important Points__**

• **Indo-Saracenic Influence**: While the buildings near the **Oval Maidan** are predominantly **Victorian Gothic**, they laid the groundwork for the **Indo-Saracenic** style, which further integrated **Islamic** and **Hindu** architectural elements like **domes**, **chhatris**, and **minarets** (e.g., the **Gateway of India** and **Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya**).

• **Urban Planning**: The **Oval Maidan** acts as a **green buffer** between two distinct architectural eras: the **Victorian Gothic** buildings to its **east** and the **Art Deco** buildings to its **west** (built on the **Backbay Reclamation** in the **1930s**).

• **Climate Adaptation**: The **verandas** were not just aesthetic; they served as **buffer zones** that prevented the interior rooms from heating up, a crucial feature before the advent of **air conditioning**. The **sloping tiled roofs** typically used **Mangalore tiles**, which were highly effective for **heavy rainfall**.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding India–Nepal water-sharing treaties:
1) The Kosi (1954) and Gandak (1959) Agreements provide for joint management of barrages, including construction, maintenance, and operation.
2) The Mahakali Treaty (1996) mandates construction of a Pancheshwar Bridge by India and allows unilateral development of river projects. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 1 is correct**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The **Kosi Agreement** was signed between **India** and **Nepal** in **1954** to manage the **Kosi River**, which is notorious for its devastating floods. This agreement facilitated the construction of the **Kosi Barrage** at **Hanuman Nagar**, located near the **Indo-Nepal border**.

• The **Gandak Agreement** was signed in **1959** for the construction of a barrage at **Valmikinagar**. Both the **Kosi** and **Gandak** agreements provide a framework for the **joint management**, **construction**, **maintenance**, and **operation** of the barrages and canal systems to ensure **flood control** and **irrigation** benefits for both countries. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***

• The **Mahakali Treaty** was signed in **February 1996**. It is an integrated treaty for the development of the **Mahakali River**, which forms a significant part of the boundary between **India** and **Nepal**.

• The treaty covers the **Sarada Barrage**, the **Tanakpur Barrage**, and the proposed **Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project**. Contrary to the statement, the treaty is based on the principle of **equal partnership** and **joint development** rather than **unilateral development**. It requires the **Pancheshwar Project** to be implemented as a joint venture. While infrastructure like bridges may be part of broader connectivity, the treaty's core mandate is **water sharing** and **power generation**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Kosi River (Sorrow of Bihar):**

• The **Kosi River** originates in the **Himalayas** and flows through **Nepal** and **India**. The **1954 agreement** was later amended in **1966** to address **Nepal's** concerns regarding its **water rights** and **sovereignty**.

• The project provides **irrigation** to approximately **11.5 lakh hectares** of land in **Bihar** and **Nepal**.

• **Gandak River:**

• Known as the **Narayani** in **Nepal**, it is a major tributary of the **Ganges**. The **1959 agreement** ensures **irrigation** for **Uttar Pradesh**, **Bihar**, and **Nepal**.

• The **Gandak Project** includes a **hydroelectric power station** at **Surajpura** in **Nepal**.

• **Mahakali Treaty (1996):**

• The **Mahakali River** is known as the **Sarda River** in **India**. The **Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project (PMP)** is the centerpiece of this treaty, designed to have an installed capacity of **6,480 MW**.

• The treaty stipulates that **India** and **Nepal** will share the **costs** of the project in proportion to the **benefits** received, particularly in terms of **power** and **irrigation**.

• **Institutional Mechanisms:**

• Bilateral water cooperation is overseen by the **Joint Committee on Water Resources (JCWR)**, which is led by the **Water Resources Secretaries** of both nations.

• The **Joint Standing Technical Committee (JSTC)** and the **Joint Committee on Inundation and Flood Management (JCIFM)** also play vital roles in managing **transboundary water issues**.

**Important Points__**

• **Article 7** of the **Mahakali Treaty** specifically mentions that neither party shall use the **Mahakali River** water in a way that causes **significant harm** to the other.

• The **Sapta Kosi High Dam Project** is another major proposed initiative between the two countries aimed at **flood control** in **North Bihar** and **hydropower generation**.

• The **India-Nepal** cooperation in the **water sector** is crucial for **regional stability**, **energy security**, and **disaster management** in the **Ganges basin**.
</ul

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the India–Bhutan Friendship Treaty signed in 2007:

1) The treaty affirms mutual respect for sovereignty and bans harmful use of each other’s territory.

2) Article 4 permits Bhutan to export arms to third countries with India’s consent.

3) The treaty promotes free trade and cultural cooperation in areas like education and health.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1 and 3 only**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **India-Bhutan Friendship Treaty** was signed in **February 2007**, replacing the earlier treaty of **1949**. This updated treaty reflects the contemporary nature of the bilateral relationship, emphasizing mutual respect for each other's **sovereignty** and **territorial integrity**.
 
• **Statement 1**: The treaty affirms that both nations shall respect each other's independence and sovereignty. It explicitly mentions that neither government shall allow the use of its territory for activities harmful to the national security and interest of the other. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Statement 2**: **Article 4** of the **2007 Treaty** pertains to the **import** of arms and ammunition. It states that the **Government of Bhutan** is free to import arms, ammunition, and machinery required for its security from or through **India**, provided the intentions are friendly and do not pose a danger to **India**. It does not grant **Bhutan** the permission to **export** arms to third countries. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Statement 3**: The treaty significantly broadens the scope of cooperation. **Article 7** establishes **free trade** and commerce between the two territories, while **Article 8** encourages cooperation in various fields including **culture**, **education**, **health**, **sports**, and **science and technology**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• The revision of the treaty was a landmark event that removed the clause from the **1949** version which stated that **Bhutan** would be 'guided by the advice' of **India** in its external relations, thereby granting **Bhutan** more **strategic autonomy**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Historical Context:** Diplomatic relations between **India** and **Bhutan** were formally established in **1968** with the appointment of a resident representative in **Thimphu**. The basic framework of their bilateral relations was the **Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation** signed in **1949**.
 
• **Strategic Importance:** **Bhutan** shares a border of approximately **699 km** with **India**, touching the states of **Sikkim**, **West Bengal**, **Assam**, and **Arunachal Pradesh**. It serves as a **buffer state** between **India** and **China**.
 
• **Economic Cooperation:** **India** is **Bhutan's** largest **trading partner**. The **hydropower** sector is the hallmark of this relationship. Several projects like the **Chukha** (336 MW), **Kurichhu** (60 MW), **Tala** (1020 MW), and **Mangdechhu** (720 MW) have been developed with **Indian** assistance.
 
• **Developmental Assistance:** **India** has been a major contributor to **Bhutan's Five-Year Plans** since their inception in **1961**. A significant portion of **India's** external aid budget is consistently allocated to **Bhutan** for infrastructure, **ICT**, and **social sectors**.
 
• **Security Cooperation:** Both countries cooperate closely on **border management**. In **2003**, the **Royal Bhutan Army** conducted **Operation All Clear** to flush out **Indian** insurgent groups (like **ULFA** and **NDFB**) operating from **Bhutanese** soil, demonstrating the strength of the security partnership.
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The **2007 Treaty** was signed by the then **External Affairs Minister** of **India**, **Pranab Mukherjee**, and the then **Crown Prince** (now King) of **Bhutan**, **Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck**.
 
• The treaty provides for **extradition** of criminals and **mutual legal assistance** in criminal matters.
 
• It also ensures that **Bhutanese** citizens in **India** and **Indian** citizens in **Bhutan** shall enjoy the same facilities regarding trade and commerce as the locals.

Consider the following statements about 'Chronicle of a Corpse Bearer' by Cyrus Mistry:**
1) Won DSC Prize for depicting marginalized Parsi communities in Mumbai.

2) Received Booker Prize for narrative innovation and postcolonial themes.

3) Awarded Sahitya Akademi in 2015.

Which of the above statements is/are correct**?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Statements 1 and 3 both are correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The novel **Chronicle of a Corpse Bearer** was written by the acclaimed **Indian author** **Cyrus Mistry** and published in **2012**. It won the **DSC Prize for South Asian Literature** in **2014**. The book is noted for its deep and empathetic portrayal of the **Khandhia** community, who are the marginalized **corpse bearers** within the **Parsi community** in **Mumbai**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• While the novel received significant critical acclaim and international recognition, it did not receive the **Booker Prize**. The **Booker Prize** is a prestigious literary award for the best novel written in **English** and published in the **UK** or **Ireland**, but this specific work was not among its winners. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Cyrus Mistry** was conferred with the **Sahitya Akademi Award** in **2015** for this novel in the **English language** category. This award is one of the highest literary honors bestowed by the **Government of India**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• The core logic of the question rests on identifying the specific literary honors received by **Cyrus Mistry** for his work that highlights the social stratification within the **Zoroastrian** faith. ***Hence, the correct answer is Statements 1 and 3 both are correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cyrus Mistry:** He is a **Mumbai-based** **playwright** and **novelist**. He is the younger brother of the famous author **Rohinton Mistry**. His writing often delves into the lives of the **Parsi** community, exploring themes of **marginalization** and **tradition**.
 
• **Book Summary:** The story is set in **pre-independence India** and follows **Phiroze Elchidana**, the son of a **Parsi priest**. Phiroze falls in love with **Sepideh**, the daughter of a **Khandhia**, and chooses to become a **corpse bearer** himself to marry her, thereby entering a life of **social exclusion** and **poverty**.
 
• **The Khandhia Community:** In the **Zoroastrian** tradition, **Khandhias** are those who carry the deceased to the **Towers of Silence** (**Doongerwadi**) for **excarnation**. Despite their vital religious role, they are often treated as **untouchables** within their own community and live in **segregated housing**.
 
• **DSC Prize for South Asian Literature:** This is an international literary prize awarded annually to writers of any **ethnicity** or **nationality**, provided the writing is about the **South Asian** region. **Cyrus Mistry** received the **$25,000** prize at the **Jaipur Literature Festival**.
 
• **Sahitya Akademi Award:** Established in **1954**, it is a literary honor in **India**, which the **Sahitya Akademi** (India's National Academy of Letters) annually confers on writers of the most outstanding books of literary merit published in any of the **24 major Indian languages**, including **English**.
 
• **Location and Context:** The novel is primarily set in **Mumbai** (formerly **Bombay**) and provides a historical look at the **Parsi** customs and the **socio-economic** struggles of the **1940s**.

questions.question:
Which of the following is **correct** for the Indian Desert region?
1. It is a sandy plain with dunes.
2. It is heavily forested.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 1**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Indian Desert**, also known as the **Thar Desert**, is located towards the western margins of the **Aravalli Hills**. It is characterized as an undulating **sandy plain** covered with various types of **sand dunes**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• This region receives very low rainfall, generally below **150 mm** per year. Due to this **arid climate** and extreme water scarcity, the region has very **low vegetation cover** and is certainly not **heavily forested**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The topography is dominated by **shifting sand dunes** and **sandy soils** that have very low organic matter. The lack of moisture prevents the growth of dense forests, limiting the flora to **thorny bushes** and **xerophytic** plants.
 
• Streams appear only during the **rainy season** and soon disappear into the sand as they do not have enough water to reach the sea. **Luni** is the only large river in this entire region.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Only 1.***

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Location and Extent:**
 
 
• The **Thar Desert** spans across the **Northwestern** part of the Indian subcontinent. About **85%** of the desert is located in **India**, primarily in the state of **Rajasthan**, while the remaining **15%** is in **Pakistan**.
 
• In India, it also extends into parts of **Gujarat**, **Haryana**, and **Punjab**.
 
 
 
• **Geological Features:**
 
 
• **Barchans**: These are **crescent-shaped sand dunes** that cover larger areas of the desert. However, **longitudinal dunes** become more prominent near the **Indo-Pakistan border**.
 
• The desert is a **northern extension** of the **Peninsular Plateau**. Evidence of marine deposits can be found at **Akal Wood Fossil Park** near **Jaisalmer**, indicating that this area was under the sea during the **Mesozoic Era**.
 
 
 
• **Climate and Vegetation:**
 
 
• The region experiences **extreme temperatures**, with very hot summers and cold winters. The **evaporation** rate is much higher than the **precipitation** rate.
 
• The natural vegetation is classified as **Tropical Thorn Forests**. Common species include **Khejri** (Prosopis cineraria), **Acacia**, and various types of **Cacti**.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• **Indira Gandhi Canal**: This is the **longest canal** in India, which has significantly changed the **ecology** and **economy** of the northern part of the **Indian Desert** by providing water for **irrigation** and drinking.
 
• **Luni River**: Originating in the **Pushkar Valley** of the **Aravalli Range**, it flows through the **Thar Desert** and ends in the marshy lands of the **Rann of Kutch** in **Gujarat**.
 
• **Saline Lakes**: The region has several salt lakes like **Sambhar**, **Didwana**, and **Pachpadra**, which are important sources of **salt production** in India.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct option:**Statement 1:** India has completed its demographic transition as both death and birth rates have declined equally.**Statement 2:** In India, although mortality rates have reduced, the birth rate remains comparatively high.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 2**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Demographic Transition Model (DTM)** is a framework that explains the transformation of countries from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as they move from a pre-industrial to an industrialized economic system. India has not yet completed its demographic transition. It is currently situated in the **late third stage** of this transition. For a transition to be considered complete (Stage 4), both birth and death rates must be low and approximately equal, leading to a stable or stationary population. **Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.**

• In India, the **Mortality Rate** (Death Rate) has seen a sharp decline over the last several decades due to significant improvements in **medical technology**, **public health services**, **vaccination programs**, and **food security**. However, the **Birth Rate**, while declining, has not fallen as rapidly as the death rate. This lag between the falling death rate and the slowly declining birth rate is a characteristic of a developing economy undergoing transition. **Hence, statement 2 is correct.**

• According to the **Sample Registration System (SRS)** data, India’s **Crude Birth Rate (CBR)** has declined significantly from about **40.8 per 1000** in **1951** to approximately **19.5 per 1000** in recent years. Simultaneously, the **Crude Death Rate (CDR)** has dropped from **25.1 per 1000** in **1951** to around **6.0 per 1000**. The gap between these two rates explains why India’s population continues to grow despite the decline in fertility.

• The **National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5)** conducted between **2019-21** revealed that India’s **Total Fertility Rate (TFR)** has reached **2.0**, which is slightly below the **Replacement Level Fertility** of **2.1**. Despite reaching this milestone, the population continues to increase due to **Population Momentum**, which is the result of a large young population entering their reproductive years.

• The completion of the demographic transition would imply that the **Natural Growth Rate** (Birth Rate minus Death Rate) is near zero or negative. India’s growth rate, though slowing down, remains positive, indicating that the transition is still in progress.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Stages of Demographic Transition:**

• **Stage 1:** High Birth Rate and High Death Rate. Population remains stable but low. India was in this stage before the **1920s**. The year **1921** is known as the **Year of the Great Divide** because, after this year, the death rate started to decline consistently.

• **Stage 2:** High Birth Rate and rapidly falling Death Rate. This leads to a **Population Explosion**. India experienced this phase between **1951 and 1981**.

• **Stage 3:** Falling Birth Rate and low Death Rate. The population still grows but at a declining rate. India is currently in this phase.

• **Stage 4:** Low Birth Rate and Low Death Rate. The population becomes stable. Countries like **Japan** and many **European nations** are in this stage or moving into Stage 5 (declining population).

• **Factors for Declining Mortality:** The eradication of epidemics like **Smallpox**, control over diseases like **Malaria** and **Cholera**, and the success of the **Green Revolution** in ensuring food availability have been primary drivers in reducing the death rate in India.

• **Factors for High Birth Rate:** Socio-economic factors such as **universal marriage**, **early marriage** age, **poverty**, **illiteracy** (especially among females), and a traditional **preference for male children** have historically kept the birth rate higher than the death rate.

• **Demographic Dividend:** India is currently enjoying a **Demographic Dividend**, where the proportion of the **working-age population** (15-64 years) is larger than the dependent population. This provides a window of economic opportunity if supported by **education**, **skill development**, and **employment**.

**Important Points__**

• **Population Momentum:** This is a crucial concept in Indian demography. Even if every couple has only two children today, the population will continue to grow for a few decades because the number of people in the **reproductive age group** is very high due to high fertility in previous generations.

• **Regional Variations:** There is a significant disparity in demographic transition within India. States like **Kerala**, **Tamil Nadu**, and **Andhra Pradesh** have reached low birth and death rates (Stage 4), while states like **Bihar**, **Uttar Pradesh**, and **Madhya Pradesh** are still in the earlier phases of Stage 3 with higher fertility rates.

• **Government Initiatives:** The **National Population Policy (NPP) 2000** was formulated with the long-term objective of achieving a stable population by **2045**, which was later revised to **2070**, consistent with the requirements of sustainable economic growth.

• **Life Expectancy:** At the time of **Independence in 1947**, the average life expectancy in India was around **32 years**. Due to the demographic transition, it has increased to approximately **70 years** as of **2023**, reflecting the success in reducing mortality.

55:T33

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about India's Biosphere Reserves:
1. All biosphere reserves are notified as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
2. Gulf of Mannar and Great Nicobar are included in the World Network of Biosphere Reserves.
3. Biosphere reserves often include core, buffer, and transition zones.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 2 and 3 are correct**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Biosphere Reserves** are designated by the **national government** and must meet a minimal set of criteria to be included in the **World Network of Biosphere Reserves (WNBR)** under **UNESCO’s Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme**. While some **Biosphere Reserves** like the **Sundarbans** or **Nanda Devi** are also **UNESCO World Heritage Sites**, these are two separate programs with different legal frameworks and objectives. Not every biosphere reserve is a **World Heritage Site**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• The **World Network of Biosphere Reserves (WNBR)** is a global network of sites that excel in biodiversity conservation and sustainable development. In **India**, out of **18** notified biosphere reserves, **12** are part of the **WNBR**. Both the **Gulf of Mannar** (located in **Tamil Nadu**) and the **Great Nicobar** (located in the **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**) are included in this prestigious international list. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• A **Biosphere Reserve** is structured into three specific zones to manage conservation and human activity effectively. The **Core Area** is a strictly protected ecosystem that contributes to the conservation of landscapes, ecosystems, and species. The **Buffer Zone** surrounds the core and is used for activities compatible with sound ecological practices, such as **environmental education** and **research**. The **Transition Area** is the outermost part where **sustainable development** practices and human settlements are permitted. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Biosphere Reserves in India:**
 
 
• There are currently **18** notified **Biosphere Reserves** in **India**, established to protect larger areas of natural habitat than a typical **National Park** or **Animal Sanctuary**.
 
• The **Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve**, established in **1986**, was the first biosphere reserve in **India**. It spans across the states of **Tamil Nadu**, **Karnataka**, and **Kerala**.
 
• The **Panna Biosphere Reserve** in **Madhya Pradesh** became the **12th** Indian reserve to be included in the **UNESCO WNBR** in **2020**.
 
• The **Gulf of Kachchh** in **Gujarat** is the **largest** biosphere reserve in **India** by area, while **Dibru-Saikhowa** in **Assam** is considered one of the **smallest**.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme:**
 
 
• Launched in **1971**, the **MAB Programme** is an intergovernmental scientific program that aims to establish a scientific basis for the improvement of relationships between people and their environments.
 
• It promotes innovative approaches to **economic development** that are socially and culturally appropriate and environmentally sustainable.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Functions of Biosphere Reserves:**
 
 
• **Conservation:** To ensure the conservation of **landscapes**, **ecosystems**, **species**, and **genetic variation**.
 
• **Development:** To foster **economic** and **human development** which is socio-culturally and ecologically sustainable.
 
• **Logistic Support:** To provide support for **research**, **monitoring**, **education**, and **information exchange** related to local, national, and global issues of conservation and development.
 
 
 
• **Zoning Details:**
 
 
• The **Core Zone** is often a **National Park** or a **Sanctuary** protected under the **Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972**. It is kept free from **human interference**.
 
• In the **Buffer Zone**, limited **tourism**, **grazing**, and **fishing** might be allowed to reduce the pressure on the core area.
 
• The **Transition Zone** is the area of **cooperation** where conservation goals and sustainable development are balanced with the help of **local communities**.

questions.question: What was the key feature of liberalization under the NEP 1991?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Abolition of industrial licensing**__.

**__Key Points__**

• **Liberalization** under the **New Economic Policy (NEP) 1991** was primarily aimed at dismantling the **License Raj**, a system of elaborate licenses, regulations, and red tape that hindered industrial growth and private enterprise for decades.

• The most significant feature of this reform was the **abolition of industrial licensing** for almost all industrial categories, except for a few strategic sectors related to **defense**, **hazardous chemicals**, and **environmental concerns**. This allowed entrepreneurs to make decisions based on market demand rather than bureaucratic approval. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***

• **Increase in agricultural subsidies** was not a part of the **1991** liberalization framework; the policy actually focused on **fiscal discipline** and reducing government expenditure to control the burgeoning **fiscal deficit**. **Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.**<

questions.question:
Which of the following are included under the scope of Article 21 as interpreted by the Supreme Court?
1. Right to sleep
2. Right to shelter
3. Right to reputation
4. Right to die
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1, 2 and 3 only**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Right to sleep**: The **Supreme Court**, in the **Ramlila Maidan Incident v. Home Secretary, Union of India (2012)**, held that the **right to sleep** is a fundamental right. The court stated that sleep is essential for a human being to maintain the biological balance and health of the body, and disturbing it constitutes a violation of **Article 21**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.*** 
• **Right to shelter**: In the case of **Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985)** and **Shantistar Builders v. Narayan Khimalal Totame (1990)**, the **Supreme Court** ruled that the **right to life** includes the **right to shelter**. It emphasized that for a human being, a house is not just a place to live but a place for physical, mental, and intellectual growth. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.*** 
• **Right to reputation**: The **Supreme Court**, in the case of **Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016)**, held that the **right to reputation** is an integral part of **Article 21**. The court observed that a person's reputation is an inseparable facet of their dignity and life. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.*** 
• **Right to die**: In the landmark judgment of **Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996)**, a five-judge bench of the **Supreme Court** held that the **right to life** under **Article 21** does not include the **right to die** or the right to be killed. While the court later allowed **passive euthanasia** under strict guidelines in the **Common Cause (2018)** case, the general "right to die" (as in suicide) is not recognized as a fundamental right. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*** 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
• **Article 21 of the Indian Constitution**: 
• It declares that "No person shall be deprived of his **life or personal liberty** except according to **procedure established by law**." This right is available to both **citizens and non-citizens**. 
• This article has been described as the "**heart of fundamental rights**" due to its wide and evolving interpretation by the judiciary. 
• **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)**: 
• This case was a turning point for **Article 21**. The **Supreme Court** established that the "**procedure established by law**" must be **just, fair, and reasonable** (introducing the American concept of **Substantive Due Process**). 
• It ruled that "**Personal Liberty**" has the widest amplitude and covers a variety of rights that go to constitute the personal liberty of a man. 
• **Other Rights under Article 21**: 
• Over the years, the **Supreme Court** has included several rights under its scope, such as the **Right to Privacy (Justice K.S. Puttaswamy case, 2017)**, **Right to a Clean Environment**, **Right to Free Legal Aid**, **Right to Education**, and **Right to Speedy Trial**. 
• It also includes the **Right against Handcuffing** and the **Right to Travel Abroad**. 
• **Protection during Emergency**: 
• By the **44th Amendment Act (1978)**, it was mandated that the enforcement of the rights guaranteed by **Articles 20 and 21** cannot be suspended even during the operation of a **National Emergency** under **Article 352**. </ul
